items.label: text
items.text: Phosphorus does not react with water.

items.label: text
items.text: Safety Note: The teacher demonstrating needs to wear goggles or a face shield, and have the room well ventilated. After igniting the phosphorous the bell-jar needs to be held down as pressure rises initially. After all the fumes have gone the evaporating basin needs to be sunk using the glass rod to prevent any unreacted phosphorous re-igniting.

items.label: text
items.text: Phosphorus is a very reactive element that reacts with the oxygen in the air to form a phosphorus oxide. This oxide is very soluble in water.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Figure 13.4 Finding the percentage of oxygen in air using phosphorus.

items.label: list_item
items.text: The apparatus shown in Figure 13.4 is set up with the piece of phosphorus on an evaporating basin, which is floating in the water.

items.label: list_item
items.text: The initial level of water is marked on the side of the bell jar with a waterproof pen or a sticker.

items.label: list_item
items.text: The bung is removed from the bell jar and the phosphorus is touched with a hot metal wire in order to ignite it.

items.label: list_item
items.text: The bung is quickly put back into the bell jar.

items.label: list_item
items.text: The phosphorus burns, the bell jar becomes filled with a white smoke (phosphorus oxide) and the level of water rises inside the bell jar. The smoke eventually clears as the phosphorus oxide dissolves in the water.

items.label: list_item
items.text: When the level of water inside the bell jar stops rising, the final level is marked.

items.label: list_item
items.text: To find how much the water level has changed, the bell jar is turned upside down, filled with water to each mark in turn and the water is poured into a large measuring cylinder.

items.label: text
items.text: It is important that there is still some phosphorus left on the evaporating basin at the end of the experiment. We have used an excess of phosphorus so that there is more than enough to react with all the oxygen. If there was no phosphorus left, then we would probably get a lower value for the percentage of oxygen in the air because not all the oxygen might have been used up.

items.label: section_header
items.text: THE COMBUSTION OF ELEMENTS IN OXYGEN

items.label: text
items.text: Some elements burn in oxygen, these reactions are called combustion reactions. Elements burn more brightly and rapidly in pure oxygen than in air because air only contains 21% oxygen.
